claims.text: The US court found Google's search business a monopoly because Judge Amit Mehta of the US District Court for the District of Columbia ruled on August 5, 2024 that Google violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act by acting as a monopolist in general search services and general search text advertising [Source: ev-1].

claims.text: The primary theory of harm was "default-distribution deals," where Google paid companies like Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla billions to be their default search engine [Source: ev-1].
Evidence showed Google paid approximately $26.3 billion for distribution in 2021, including roughly 36% of Safari search-ad revenue to Apple [Source: ev-1].
The court determined this conduct created an exclusionary loop where defaults create scale, which creates data, leading to quality that protects the default position against rivals [Source: ev-1].

As a result, on August 5, 2015 (noted as 2025-08-05 in evidence), Judge Mehta ordered structural remedies requiring Google to sell Chrome and prohibiting it from paying for default search placement through revenue-sharing agreements [Source: ev-1].

claims.text: The ruling also includes limits on acquisitions and AI-related investments [Source: ev-1].
Google appealed to the DC Circuit in 2025, arguing that the trial court punished procompetitive innovation; as of 2025, the final outcome remained pending [Source: ev-1].
